part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: With the kings far apart, take the opposition from afar. With every step of the other king, it turns into direct opposition.
part.diagonal.title: Diagonal opposition
part.diagonal.summary: When the file is out of reach, the opposition also works along a diagonal.
step.t_diagonal: The black king watches the key squares of the e3-pawn. The natural 1.Ke4 looks good, but it is not. Which square leaves the black king without a good reply?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The kings need not be on the same file: a diagonal works too, with one square between them.
step.t_diagonal.hint2: After coming in along the diagonal, wherever the black king goes, look to face him again, from any side.
step.diagonal: Until now the kings were on the same file. Now they are not, and the link between them is the diagonal. 1.Ke4 looks natural, but after 1...Ke6 it is the black king that has the direct opposition, and the e3-pawn does not get through. The correct entry is 1.Kf4: the kings stand on the f4-e5-d6 diagonal, with one square between them and Black to move. After 1.Kf4 Ke6, the white king answers with 2.Ke4!, face to face, and Black has to give way. From there the white king answers every move by keeping one square between the kings, on the same file or the same rank.
step.d_diagonal: Watch the diagonal turn into direct opposition.
step.d_diagonal.m1: 1.Kf4. Kings on the diagonal f4, e5, d6, one square in between, and Black to move.
step.d_diagonal.m2: 1...Ke6. The black king moves in front of the pawn to block the e-file. If White played the natural 2.e4?, Black would draw with 2...Kf6! With f5 between the kings and White to move, the direct opposition would pass to Black.
step.d_diagonal.m3: 2.Ke4! The only winning move: the kings stand face to face on the e-file, one square apart, and Black is to move. That is the direct opposition.
step.d_diagonal.m4: 2...Kd6. The black king has to give way and goes to d6, from where it still guards d5 and e5; the f5-square is left free.
step.d_diagonal.m5: 3.Kf5. The key square that was left free. With the king here, the e3-pawn queens.
step.diagonalMove: Play White and find the best move. The black king watches the key squares of the e3-pawn.
step.diagonalMove.hint:
First look for diagonal opposition. After the reply, identify the rank or file on which your king can prevent the opposing king from approaching and reach a key square.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The diagonal entry prepares useful opposition; the pawn advance and direct approach give the defender the time it needs.
If White played 1.e4?, Black would reply 1...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.e4 Ke5 2.Ke2 Kxe4.
If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ke6 2.Kd3 Kd5.

At move 2
The key square along the rank is decisive; a pawn check cannot replace the king’s position.
If White played 2.e4+?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.e4+ Ke6 3.e5 Kd7.
step.diagonalMove.done:
The right entry: 1.Kf4 took the opposition along the diagonal and, after 1...Kd5, 2.Kf5 reached a key square, with the kings on the same rank and e5 between them.

The main line is 1.Kf4 Kd5 2.Kf5.
part.defend.title: In defence
part.defend.summary: The defender uses the same rule. He takes the opposition from afar, even by stepping back, and follows the attacking king.
step.t_carlsenSo: Now a real game, from the defender's side. {{Stavanger|stavanger}}, 2017, {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}}: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, with White, against {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}. The knights came off on move 53, and So was a pawn down, two white pawns against one. The white king wants to get in and capture the h6-pawn. Only one move draws. Which one?
step.t_carlsenSo.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the f-file.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint2: Two squares in between is an even number: on the move, you can make it odd, even by stepping back.
step.defend:
At {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, with White, faced {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, with Black. After the knights were exchanged on move 53, So was a pawn down and had to defend the h6-pawn. The black king is on f6; the white king, on f3.

Opposition also serves the side with less material. The defending king wants to stop the attacking king from gaining space to support the pawns or attack h6.

In the game, 55...Kf7! left f4, f5 and f6 between the kings, with White to move. When the white king changed file, So followed: 56.Ke3 Ke7 57.Kd3 Kd7. After 58.Kc4, 58...Ke6 went back towards the pawns: defending does not require keeping the same distance throughout.

Now White has a single pawn, on g3, and the black king must deny f5, g5 and h5. The premature-approach example starts with the black king on f6 and White’s on f3. After 1.Kf4 Kg6 2.Kg4, White has the opposition and wins: the black king controls the squares ahead, but has to move and, by giving way on one side, lets the white king in on the other.

What to do: retreat to f7, far enough to answer the white king’s advance. After 1...Kf7 2.Ke4, Black replies 2...Ke6, face to face, or 2...Kg6, and the white king does not get in.
step.d_carlsenSo: The moves of the game. For the white king’s first three steps, So keeps his king on the white king’s file, with three squares between them.
step.d_carlsenSo.m1: 55...Kf7! He steps back and takes the distant opposition: f4, f5 and f6 in between, and White to move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m2: 56.Ke3. {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} changes file, trying to get in along the e-file.
step.d_carlsenSo.m3: 56...Ke7! So changes file with him: three squares in between again, now on the e-file.
step.d_carlsenSo.m4: 57.Kd3. {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} tries the d-file. If So does not follow now, he loses: 57...Kd7 is again the only move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m5: 57...Kd7! Facing him again, from afar. The white king moves, but gains no ground.
step.d_carlsenSo.m6: 58.Kc4. {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} goes up the c-file, to come in on the queenside.
step.d_carlsenSo.m7: 58...Ke6! The black king comes back close to the pawns, and the white king has no way in. The game was drawn on move 63.
step.defendMove: Play Black and find the best move. Now White has a single pawn, on g3.
step.defendMove.hint:
Defending may require a retreat. Look for a square on the white king’s file that leaves an odd number of squares between the kings and White to move. If the pawn advances, check its key squares again.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The defence must retreat to the correct distance. Moving closer or retreating too far lets the white king gain ground.
If Black played 1...Kf6?, White would reply 2.Kf4 and win. The line would be 1...Kf6 2.Kf4 Kg6 3.Kg4.
If Black played 1...Kf8?, White would reply 2.Kf4 and win. The line would be 1...Kf8 2.Kf4 Kf7 3.Kg5.

At move 2
The opposition must adapt to the white king’s new file. There is more than one defence, but not every nearby square works.
If Black played 2...Kf6?, White would reply 3.Kf4 and win. The line would be 2...Kf6 3.Kf4 Kg6 4.Kg4.
If Black played 2...Kg7?, White would reply 3.Kf5 and win. The line would be 2...Kg7 3.Kf5 Kh6 4.g4.

At move 3
After the pawn advance, occupying the key square matters more than keeping the previous distance.
If Black played 3...Kf7?, White would reply 4.Kf5 and win. The line would be 3...Kf7 4.Kf5 Kg7 5.Kg5.
step.defendMove.done:
A sound defence: 1...Kf7 left f4, f5 and f6 between the kings, with White to move, and followed the change of file. After 3.g4 the key squares become f6, g6 and h6, and 3...Kf6 occupies one of them. 2...Kg6 also draws, because the black king still watches f5, g5 and h5.

The main line is 1...Kf7 2.Ke4 Ke6 3.g4 Kf6.
2...Kg6 also works.
At the third decision, 3...Kf6 occupies the square needed for the defense.
part.lateral.title: Lateral opposition
part.lateral.summary: The opposition also works along a rank, near and far, in attack and in defence.
step.t_euwe: Now the kings face each other on the same rank. In The Hague in 1928, the World Amateur Championship was held alongside the Olympiad as a separate individual competition. In this game, {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}} had White against {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}. The rooks were exchanged on move 47, leaving each side with one pawn. The struggle is to reach the opposing pawn first: your king is heading for a5, while the black king threatens to reach c2. Only one move wins. Which move is it?
step.t_euwe.hint1: The kings can also face each other on the same rank.
step.t_euwe.hint2: Count the squares between the kings on the fifth rank after your move.
step.lateral: So far the kings faced each other head on or along a diagonal; {{Euwe|max-euwe}} used the rank. He played 49.Kb5, attacking the a5-pawn and placing the kings on the fifth rank with three squares between them and Black to move. This is distant opposition along the rank. Notice the order: first reach a useful rank, then follow the opposing king’s changes without abandoning your pawns. In the line, after capturing a5, the white king returns towards the c2-pawn. Following the other king makes sense only if that route also protects your own pawns.
step.d_euwe: The moves of the game: {{Euwe|max-euwe}} always stays on the black king's rank.
step.d_euwe.m1: 49.Kb5! The only winning move. Kings on b5 and f5, three squares in between, and Black to move.
step.d_euwe.m3: 50.Kxa5! The pawn falls, and the kings again have three squares in between, a5 and e5, with Black to move.
step.d_euwe.m4: 50...Kd4. He goes further down and threatens 51...Kc3, attacking the c2-pawn.
step.d_euwe.m5: 51.Kb4! Kings on b4 and d4, one square in between, and Black to move: lateral opposition, and c3 is shut to him.
step.d_euwe.m6: 51...Kd5. With no way through c3, he steps back. Every move loses: the white king is already in front of the pawn.
step.d_euwe.m7: 52.Kb5. The white king goes up in front of the pawn, towards b6 and c6. {{Euwe|max-euwe}} went on with 53.c4, 54.Kb6 and 55.Kc6, and the game ended there, a win for White.
step.lateralDefend: Play Black and find the best move. The white king wants to support the d2-pawn.
step.lateralDefend.hint:
Count the distance along the rank. Follow the white king’s descent without allowing it to reach the key squares before you.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The defending king needs to reach the same rank in time.
If Black played 1...Ke7?, White would reply 2.Kb5 and win. The line would be 1...Ke7 2.Kb5 Kd6 3.Kc4.
If Black played 1...Kf6?, White would reply 2.Kb5 and win. The line would be 1...Kf6 2.Kb5 Ke6 3.Kc5.

At move 2
Lateral opposition prevents access to the key squares; a difference of one square can open the route.
If Black played 2...Kd6?, White would reply 3.Kc4 and win. The line would be 2...Kd6 3.Kc4 Kc6 4.d3.
If Black played 2...Ke5?, White would reply 3.Kc5 and win. The line would be 2...Ke5 3.Kc5 Kf5 4.d4.

At move 3
Following along the rank keeps a barrier between the attacking king and the decisive squares.
If Black played 3...Kd6?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Kd6 4.Kc4 Kc6 5.d3.
If Black played 3...Ke4?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Ke4 4.Kc4 Ke5 5.Kc5.
step.lateralDefend.done:
Defence along the rank: lateral opposition maintained a barrier in front of the decisive squares. Following along the rank can require retreating before facing the king.

The main line is 1...Ke6 2.Kb5 Kd5 3.Kb4 Kd4.
The replies 2...Kd5 and 3...Kd4 follow the change of rank and maintain the barrier.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: With blocked pawns on both wings, obtain opposition before choosing the route in.
step.t_capablanca: Locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever reaches an enemy pawn first wins. Think: which white king move makes sure of getting there first?
step.t_capablanca.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the e-file. With an even number, the side to move can take the opposition.
step.t_capablanca.hint2: Six squares in between and your move: after your move an odd number must be left.
step.capablanca: Now there are pawns on both sides, and the target is not queening: it is the other side's pawn. This is the example {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} chose, in Chess Fundamentals, to show the value of the opposition. Each side has two blocked pawns, b4 against b5 and h4 against h5, and the kings are on e1 and e8, with six squares between them. An even number: whoever is to move takes the opposition, and whoever takes the opposition wins, because he reaches the other side's pawn first. 1.Ke2 is the only move that wins. After 1.Ke2 Ke7, only 2.Ke3! keeps the opposition: three squares remain between the kings, e4, e5 and e6, and Black is to move.
step.d_capablanca: Watch distant opposition become direct. The preparation for outflanking will be examined in the next section.
step.d_capablanca.m1: 1.Ke2. Five squares in between, and Black to move.
step.d_capablanca.m2: 1...Ke7. The black king advances down the e-file, aiming to shorten the distance and take the opposition itself. If White answered 2.Kd3?, leaving the file, Black would draw with 2...Kf6.
step.d_capablanca.m3: 2.Ke3! It is the only winning move: there are three squares between the kings, e4, e5 and e6, and Black is to move again.
step.d_capablanca.m4: 2...Ke6. The black king advances again and leaves only two squares between the kings, with White to move. Going diagonally would be natural, but 3.Kd4? Kd6! or 3.Kf4? Kf6! would give Black the direct opposition, with White to move, and it would be a draw.
step.d_capablanca.m5: 3.Ke4! Direct opposition, with one square between the kings and Black to move; now Black has to leave the file.
step.capablancaMove: Play White and find the best move. This time the black king leaves the file on its very first move.
step.capablancaMove.hint:
First consider who will have to give way on the kings’ file. If the opposing king changes file, compare a diagonal step with approaching in a straight line: what matters is the opposition after its reply.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The first step must establish distant opposition before choosing a wing.
If White played 1.Kd2?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd2 Kf7 2.Kc3 Ke6.
If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd7 2.Ke3 Ke7.

At move 2
The black king’s change of file requires recalculating the opposition after its reply.
If White played 2.Ke3?, Black would reply 2...Ke7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ke3 Ke7 3.Kd3 Kf6.
If White played 2.Kf3?, Black would reply 2...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf3 Kf7 3.Ke3 Ke7.

At move 3
After the lateral waiting move, it is time to return to the file at the correct distance.
If White played 3.Kd4?, Black would reply 3...Kd6 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kd4 Kd6 4.Ke4 Ke6.
If White played 3.Ke4?, Black would reply 3...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Ke4 Ke6 4.Kd4 Kf5.
step.capablancaMove.done:
Opposition regained: after 1...Kf8, 2.Kd3 waited off the file; when the black king came back to e7, 3.Ke3 restored three squares between the kings, with Black to move. 2.Kf2 also wins, because it leaves five squares between the kings on the f-file and Black to move; 2.Kf3?, however, would leave only four, and 2...Kf7 would draw. Had Black stayed on the e-file, the answer from the example would apply: 1.Ke2 Ke7 2.Ke3!

The main line is 1.Ke2 Kf8 2.Kd3 Ke7 3.Ke3.
2.Kf2 also works.
part.edge.title: Lateral approach
part.edge.summary: The squares controlled by the pawns show how to follow the opposing king.
step.t_edge: The target is the c6-pawn. 1.Kd6 looks like the shortest way. Is it?
step.t_edge.hint1: After 1.Kd6, where does the black king stand, and whose move is it?
step.t_edge.hint2: The kings are on the fifth rank; count the squares between them.
step.edge:
In the outflanking example the kings had room in the centre; now the edge restricts their routes. This training position comes from a study on distant opposition by Brandon2021.

1.Kd6? Kb6! and the kings stand on the same rank, with c6 between them and White to move: the white king does not get through, and it is a draw.

The right move is to step away: 1.Kf5! That leaves four squares between the kings, b5, c5, d5 and e5, and Black to move, but the black king cannot stay on the fifth rank, because b5 is covered by the c4-pawn. It has to go up, and the white king goes up with it, keeping three squares between them. Then the kings climb together on the same rank, and at the top the white king uses the edge to gain the move.
step.d_edge: Watch the kings climb on the same rank.
step.d_edge.m1: 1.Kf5! The white king steps away: the kings stand on a5 and f5, with four squares between them, and Black to move. The black king cannot answer on b5, which the c4-pawn covers.
step.d_edge.m2: 1...Kb6. The black king has to leave the fifth rank: b5 and b4 are covered by the c4- and a3-pawns. He goes up. Here is a common trap: the natural 2.Ke5? brings the king closer, but after 2...Kb7! Black draws; if the white king goes on to d6, 3...Kb6 puts the kings face to face on the sixth rank with White to move. What wins is 2.Kf6: the white king goes up as well and keeps the opposition along the rank.
step.d_edge.m3: 2.Kf6. The white king goes up with it: the kings stand on b6 and f6, with three squares between them, and Black to move. The c6-pawn stands on one of those squares, but the count is the same.
step.d_edge.m4: 2...Kb7. The black king goes up to b7, and the white king goes up with it to keep three squares between them on the same rank.
step.d_edge.m5: 3.Kf7. The kings are on the seventh rank, with three squares between them, and Black is still the one to move.
step.edgeMove: Play White and find the best move. The target is still the c6-pawn.
step.edgeMove.hint:
The shortest route to the pawn may surrender the opposition. Observe the squares your pawns deny the opposing king and look for a way to keep a route in from the side.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The closeness of c6 is misleading: access depends on opposition and the squares denied by the pawns.
If White played 1.Kd6?, Black would reply 1...Kb6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd6 Kb6 2.Ke5 Ka7.
If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ka6 2.Kd3 Ka5.

At move 2
After the black king goes to a6, the route in must be kept along the sixth rank. Returning to the fifth or fourth gives the defender time to reorganise the opposition.
If White played 2.Ke4?, Black would reply 2...Kb6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ke4 Kb6 3.Kd3 Ka5.
If White played 2.Ke5?, Black would reply 2...Ka7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ke5 Ka7 3.Ke4 Ka6.
If White played 2.Kg5?, Black would reply 2...Ka7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kg5 Ka7 3.Kf4 Ka6.

At move 3
Going forward without counting the turn gives away lateral opposition; approaching along the rank preserves access.
If White played 3.Kd7?, Black would reply 3...Kb7 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kd7 Kb7 4.Kd6 Kb6.
step.edgeMove.done:
Entry preserved: lateral opposition kept access to c6. Distance from the target matters less than the key squares available after the opponent’s reply.

The main line is 1.Kf5 Ka6 2.Ke6 Kb6 3.Kd6.
2.Kg6 also works.
3.Kf6 also works.
ex.e09: Play White and find the best move. Your king starts in the corner, far from the d2-pawn. Find the first two king moves against the reply shown, preparing the approach through opposition.
ex.e09.hint:
First the black king's file, from afar. Then, every time he moves, shorten the distance facing him.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre.
If White played 1.d3?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6.
If White played 1.d4?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6.

At move 2
The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence.
If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5.
ex.e09.solution:
1.Kg2! takes distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares between the kings. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! maintains opposition on the f-file, now with three intervening squares. The exercise ends here: you have prepared the approach and preserved the win, but a game would still require conversion.

A continuation using the technique studied shows how to reduce the distance: 2...Ke6 3.Ke4 Kd6 4.Kd4. The kings reach direct opposition beside the pawn. If White started with the pawn or with another king move, Black would draw.

These do not work either:

At move 1: The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre. If White played 1.d3?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6. If White played 1.d4?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6.

At move 2: The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence. If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5.
ex.e11: Play Black and find the best move. The white pawn is still on the second rank, and your king must stop the white king from reaching the key squares. Keep up the defence through the replies shown, adjusting the opposition when the opponent changes file.
ex.e11.hint:
Choose the distance that keeps the opposing king away from the key squares. Defence sometimes requires a retreat; after the opponent approaches, it may require shortening the distance. Recheck the kings’ alignment and whose turn it will be after each reply.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Distant opposition must be obtained on the white king’s file, at the correct distance; a difference of one file or rank opens the approach.
If Black played 1...Ke8?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Ke8 2.Kd2 Kd7 3.Kc3.
If Black played 1...Kf7?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Kf7 2.Kd2 Ke6 3.Kc3.

At move 2
After the change of file, the defence must shorten the distance on the correct axis.
If Black played 2...Kd7?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Kd7 3.Kc3 Kd6 4.Kc4.
If Black played 2...Ke6?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Ke6 3.Kc3 Kd5 4.Kb4.

At move 3
Giving way on the file lets the white king choose a route to the key squares.
If Black played 3...Kc5?, White would reply 4.Kc3 and win. The line would be 3...Kc5 4.Kc3 Kb5 5.Kd4.
If Black played 3...Kc6?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Kc6 4.Kc4 Kb6 5.Kd5.

At move 4
The defence must keep the barrier in front of the white king; escaping sideways or retreating gives away decisive space.
If Black played 4...Kc6?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Kc6 5.Kc4 Kb6 6.Kd5.
If Black played 4...Ke4?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Ke4 5.Kc4 Ke5 6.Kc5.
ex.e11.solution:
1...Ke7! Kings on e1 and e7, five squares between them, White to move: the distant opposition is yours. After 2.Kd2, 2...Kd6!, with three squares between; after 3.Kd3, 3...Kd5!, face to face; and after 4.Kc3, 4...Kc5! The white king never reaches the key squares of the c2-pawn, b4, c4 and d4. Any other first move lets the white king take the opposition, and at every step of the defence only one move holds.

These do not work either:

At move 1: Distant opposition must be obtained on the white king’s file, at the correct distance; a difference of one file or rank opens the approach. If Black played 1...Ke8?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Ke8 2.Kd2 Kd7 3.Kc3. If Black played 1...Kf7?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Kf7 2.Kd2 Ke6 3.Kc3.

At move 2: After the change of file, the defence must shorten the distance on the correct axis. If Black played 2...Kd7?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Kd7 3.Kc3 Kd6 4.Kc4. If Black played 2...Ke6?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Ke6 3.Kc3 Kd5 4.Kb4.

At move 3: Giving way on the file lets the white king choose a route to the key squares. If Black played 3...Kc5?, White would reply 4.Kc3 and win. The line would be 3...Kc5 4.Kc3 Kb5 5.Kd4. If Black played 3...Kc6?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Kc6 4.Kc4 Kb6 5.Kd5.

At move 4: The defence must keep the barrier in front of the white king; escaping sideways or retreating gives away decisive space. If Black played 4...Kc6?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Kc6 5.Kc4 Kb6 6.Kd5. If Black played 4...Ke4?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Ke4 5.Kc4 Ke5 6.Kc5.
ex.e13: Play White and find the best move. Black has two pawns against one, and the black king threatens to enter along the second rank and capture e3. Keep the pawn protected as the kings change rank.
ex.e13.hint:
Look for a way to reach the black king’s rank without approaching too early. Opposition also works along a rank and from a distance: consider how far apart the kings will be and whose turn it will be.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Approaching before reaching the correct rank lets the black king establish favourable opposition and seek a way in.
If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd2 and win. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd2 2.Kf3 Ke1.
If White played 1.Kf3?, Black would reply 1...Kd1 and win. The line would be 1.Kf3 Kd1 2.Kf2 Kd2.

At move 2
The e3-pawn must be protected while following the black king along the rank. Moving away allows the pawn to be captured immediately.
If White played 2.Kf1?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kf1 Kxe3 3.Ke1 f4.
If White played 2.Kg2?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kg2 Kxe3 3.Kf1 f4.

At move 3
The e3-pawn is part of the defence: advancing it gives away a capture and leaves Black with a passed pawn.
If White played 3.e4?, Black would reply 3...dxe4 and win. The line would be 3.e4 dxe4 4.Ke1 e3.
ex.e13.solution:
1.Kg1! Kings on c1 and g1, three squares between them, d1, e1 and f1, and Black to move: the distant opposition along the rank is yours. After 1...Kd2, 2.Kf2!, on the same rank with one square between; after 2...Kd3, 3.Kf3! The black king never sets foot on e2 or e4, and the e3-pawn stays. 1.Kf2? looks more active, but after 1...Kd2 it is your move and Black has the opposition; 2.Kf1? loses to 2...Kd1! {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} shows the same defence, with the pawns one file further right, in example 28 of Chess Fundamentals.

These do not work either:

At move 1: Approaching before reaching the correct rank lets the black king establish favourable opposition and seek a way in. If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd2 and win. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd2 2.Kf3 Ke1. If White played 1.Kf3?, Black would reply 1...Kd1 and win. The line would be 1.Kf3 Kd1 2.Kf2 Kd2.

At move 2: The e3-pawn must be protected while following the black king along the rank. Moving away allows the pawn to be captured immediately. If White played 2.Kf1?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kf1 Kxe3 3.Ke1 f4. If White played 2.Kg2?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kg2 Kxe3 3.Kf1 f4.

At move 3: The e3-pawn is part of the defence: advancing it gives away a capture and leaves Black with a passed pawn. If White played 3.e4?, Black would reply 3...dxe4 and win. The line would be 3.e4 dxe4 4.Ke1 e3.
key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.diagonal: The opposition works along the diagonal too: the white king stands on the same diagonal as the black king and, step by step, turns it into face-to-face opposition.
key.capablanca: {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}'s example: locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
key.carlsenSo: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White, faced {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017. Black was a pawn down and needed to prevent the white king from entering. The black king retreated to obtain distant opposition and followed its opponent from file to file; the game ended in a draw.
key.euweWhitaker: {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}}, playing White, faced {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}, playing Black, in The Hague in 1928. The white king obtained distant opposition on the same rank as the black king, approaching the opposing pawn without allowing an equivalent race on the other wing. White won; observe how the kings’ relative positions help reach the target.
history:
Opposition is the contest between kings to force the opponent to give up space; it can begin at a distance or along a diagonal. The goal is to reach an important square, capture a pawn, or prevent an opposing entry. In his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} explains the topic as an author through pawn-ending examples.

The technique also appears in games: at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, defended an ending a pawn down against {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White. The black king followed the white king from a distance, and the game ended in a draw. Just a few pieces can conceal a precise contest for space and time.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3, and the black king on e6, in front of the key squares. Find the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
step.d_outflank.m1: 4.Kf4. The king follows on the f-file and controls g4 and g5. This keeps the route to the h4-pawn closed.
step.d_outflank.m2: 4...Kg6. The black king leaves the f-file to remain close to the h5-pawn. The route through the center is now open.
step.d_outflank.m3: 5.Ke5. Now going round has a safe goal: approach Black’s b5-pawn through the centre while the black king is far away. White’s b4-pawn is covered on the way, and the earlier preparation prevented an equivalent race against h4.
part.outflank.title: Outflanking
part.outflank.summary: Before going around the other side, prevent the opposing king from reaching your pawns.
step.t_outflank: Direct opposition has already been reached, and the black king has stepped away to f6. Black’s b5-pawn looks close, but White’s h4-pawn also needs protecting. Should the king go round at once or follow once more?
step.t_outflank.hint1: Compare your king’s route to b5 with the opposing king’s route to h4.
step.t_outflank.hint2: Before changing wings, look for a way to deny the black king squares on its approach.
step.outflank: Going round means passing along the wing the enemy king has left free. The passage is only useful if it does not hand over an equally important target. In this position 4.Kf4 keeps the opposition and covers the approach to h4. After 4...Kg6, 5.Ke5 switches the target to Black’s b5-pawn. The pawn structure decides when to follow and when to go round.
step.d_outflank: Watch first how the black king is restricted, then the entry through the centre.
step.outflankMove: Play White and find the best move. White’s h4-pawn also needs protecting.
step.outflankMove.hint:
Look at the target the opposing king could reach if you changed wings now.

These do not work either:

At move 4
Switching early to the queenside lets the black king advance toward h4. That counterplay must first be restricted.
If White played 4.Kd4?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd4 Kf5 5.Kc5 Kg4.
If White played 4.Kd5?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd5 Kf5 5.Kd4 Kf4.

At move 5
After restricting the kingside, more than one central route wins. Retreating to g3, however, lets Black regain activity.
If White played 5.Kg3?, Black would reply 5...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.Kg3 Kf5 6.Kf3 Ke5.
step.outflankMove.done:
Going round at the right time: 4.Kf4 took g4 and g5 away from the black king, and only then did the white king enter through the centre with 5.Ke5. 5.Ke4 also wins: the h4-pawn covers g5, and the king covers f5.

The main line is 4.Kf4 Kg6 5.Ke5.
5.Ke4 also works.
step.d_edgeCorner.m1: 1.Ke8. Waiting prepares the return to the seventh rank after the defender’s reply.
step.d_edgeCorner.m2: 1...Ka7. The defender returns to the seventh rank. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Kd7? shortens the distance, but 2...Kb7! leaves the kings on b7 and d7, with one square between them and White to move; the opposition belongs to Black, and Black draws. What wins is 2.Ke7, with three squares between the kings and Black to move.
step.d_edgeCorner.m3: 2.Ke7. Three squares separate the kings and Black moves. This opposition prepares entry, but does not yet capture a pawn.
part.edgeCorner.title: At the edge
part.edgeCorner.summary: A waiting square makes it possible to regain the opposition without abandoning the target.
step.t_edgeCorner: The kings have already climbed the board. The white king is on f7 and wants to reach c6; the black king has returned to b6. Which waiting move lets White continue the struggle for opposition at the edge?
step.t_edgeCorner.hint1: The square nearest the target is not always the one that preserves the route in.
step.t_edgeCorner.hint2: Consider the rank still available behind your king and the opponent’s replies on the seventh.
step.edgeCorner:
The black king protects c6 and tries to answer the white king’s approaches along the same rank. Near the edge, the waiting move must produce a useful entry.

The line 1.Ke8 Ka7 2.Ke7 leaves three squares between the kings on the seventh rank, with Black to move. After 2...Kb7 the plan changes: it is time to use d7 as a passage, keeping Black on move.

With 3.Kd7! Kb6 4.Kd6, the black king has to leave b6. If it chooses 4...Ka5, 5.Kxc5 captures a pawn and keeps the white king protecting c4. Pressing c6 does not mean it will be the first pawn captured: after the capture, the safety of the white pawn counts too.

Compare 3.Kd6? Kb6! The same alignment on the sixth rank arises with White to move, and Black draws. The regained opposition must turn into an entry at the right moment.
step.d_edgeCorner: First White regains the opposition; then uses the d7 passage to force the black king to give way next to the pawns.
step.edgeCornerMove: Play White and find the best move. The white king is on f7; the black one, on b6, protects c6.
step.edgeCornerMove.hint: After waiting, compare who will move after your entry. The defender must not be able to answer on the same rank and pass the obligation to move back to you.
step.edgeCornerMove.done: In the main line, the wait 1.Ke8 regained the opposition on the seventh rank, and 3.Kd7 went through the useful passage, with Black to move. Opposition served to make the defender give way near c6 and c5; the capture depends on its chosen reply.
step.err_diagonalKing.m1: 1...Ke6. Black faces the opposing king, with one square between them and White to move.
step.err_diagonalKing.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king must look for another route; the direct approach did not secure a way through.
step.err_diagonalKing.m3: 2...Kd5. The defence follows onto the new file and keeps direct opposition. The position is drawn.
step.err_diagonalKing: The white king chose the direct entry on e4. Follow the opposition obtained by Black.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m1: 1...Ke6. The king escapes the check and continues preventing entry in front of the pawn.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m2: 2.e5. The pawn advances again. The white king has still not established a winning position.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m3: 2...Kd7. The king retreats safely; the defence preserves the draw. The active-looking check did not compensate for missing the key square.
step.err_diagonalCheck: The white pawn has just given check, but the king did not occupy the available key square. See why the check is not decisive.
step.err_defendClose.m1: 1.Kf4. White takes direct opposition, with Black to move.
step.err_defendClose.m2: 1...Kg6. The black king gives way on the file. White already has a winning continuation.
step.err_defendClose.m3: 2.Kg4. The white king follows and maintains opposition, preparing to enter the key squares.
step.err_defendClose: Black brought the king closer too early. Now follow White, which can gain space.
step.err_defendRetreat.m1: 1.Kf5. The white king reaches a key square for the pawn and preserves the win.
step.err_defendRetreat.m2: 1...Kg7. The black king tries to stay in front, but has already conceded a decisive position.
step.err_defendRetreat.m3: 2.Kg5. The white king occupies another key square and keeps the winning position.
step.err_defendRetreat: Black retreated when it needed to guard the key squares. Watch the white king enter.
step.err_lateralFile.m1: 1.Kb5. The white king descends towards the important squares for supporting its pawn.
step.err_lateralFile.m2: 1...Ke6. Black tries to correct the route, but White already has time to advance.
step.err_lateralFile.m3: 2.Kc5. The white king gains ground. The defence arrived too late to maintain the lateral barrier.
step.err_lateralFile: The black king moved down without adjusting its file. Now follow the space gained by White.
step.err_lateralDistance.m1: 1.Kc4. The white king reaches a key square for the d2-pawn.
step.err_lateralDistance.m2: 1...Kc6. The black king tries to obtain opposition on the file, but the important entry has already happened.
step.err_lateralDistance.m3: 2.d3. The pawn advances with support from its king’s position. White’s advantage remains winning.
step.err_lateralDistance: The black king kept the wrong distance along the rank. Follow White’s entry.
step.err_capablanca.m1: 1...Ke7. Black returns to the e-file with three squares between the kings and White to move.
step.err_capablanca.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king changes direction, but can no longer force the same route through.
step.err_capablanca.m3: 2...Kf6. The defence can reorganise on the other wing. The position remains drawn despite the white king’s apparent initiative.
step.err_capablanca: The white king advanced straight ahead after the opposing king changed file. See who obtains the opposition.
step.err_edge.m1: 1...Kb6. The black king takes lateral opposition: one square between the kings, with White to move.
step.err_edge.m2: 2.Ke5. The white king turns back to look for another route. The earlier approach did not secure the capture.
step.err_edge.m3: 2...Ka7. The black king maintains a sufficient defence. Access to the pawn has not been won.
step.err_edge: The white king rushed directly to d6. The pawn looks close, but opposition determines access.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint3: Stepping sideways abandons the opposition relationship and allows the white king to advance with its pawns. Both 55...Ke5 56.Ke3 Kd5 57.Kf4 and 55...Kg6 56.Ke4 Kf6 57.Kd5 leave White with a winning position. Consider how to preserve the distance before contesting lateral space.
step.t_euwe.hint3: Advancing the pawn or approaching through the center does not settle the race between the two targets: 49.c3 Ke4 50.Kb3 Kd3 and 49.Kd5 a4 50.Kc4 Ke4 lead to drawn positions. Compare the kings’ ranks and the route to a5 before choosing the advance.
step.t_diagonal.hint3:
Advancing the pawn without support or approaching through the apparently most direct square does not guarantee a key square. The black king can reorganize the opposition.

If White played 1.e4?, Black would reply 1...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.e4 Ke5 2.Ke2 Kxe4.

If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ke6 2.Kd3 Kd5.
step.t_capablanca.hint3:
Stepping sideways before restricting the opposing king allows it to follow. The change of target must be prepared through the contest for opposition.

If White played 1.Kd2?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd2 Kf7 2.Kc3 Ke6.

If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd7 2.Ke3 Ke7.
step.t_outflank.hint3:
Switching early to the queenside leaves the black king counterplay against h4. Restrict that access before going around.

If White played 4.Kd4?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd4 Kf5 5.Kc5 Kg4.

If White played 4.Kd5?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd5 Kf5 5.Kd4 Kf4.
step.t_edge.hint3:
Approaching without preparing opposition or retreating toward the center lets the black king continue blocking the entry. Compare access to the target after Black’s reply.

If White played 1.Kd6?, Black would reply 1...Kb6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd6 Kb6 2.Ke5 Ka7.

If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ka6 2.Kd3 Ka5.
step.t_edgeCorner.hint3:
An immediate approach lets Black follow along the edge. A waiting move must prepare a relationship between the kings that forces the defender to give way.

If White played 1.Ke6?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke6 Ka6 2.Ke5 Ka7.

If White played 1.Ke7?, Black would reply 1...Ka7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke7 Ka7 2.Kd6 Kb6.
step.d_capablancaReturn: The kings are on d3 and e7, as in the practice after Black’s second move, and White is to move. The white king should not go up at once: first it regains the opposition on the file to which the black king returned.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m1: 3.Ke3! The king moves along the rank and leaves three squares between the kings on the e-file, with Black to move. This is the only move that preserves the win. If White advanced directly, Black would draw: 3.Kd4 Kd6 4.Ke4 Ke6 returns direct opposition to Black; 3.Ke4 Ke6 4.Kd4 Kf5 lets the black king approach h4.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m2: 3...Ke6. The black king reduces the distance. There are now two squares between the kings, and White can respond on the same axis.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m3: 4.Ke4! With the kings on e4 and e6 and Black to move, White takes direct opposition. The position remains winning: the lateral waiting move prepared an effective approach rather than merely adding a step toward the pawns.
part.protectPawn.title: Protecting the pawn
part.protectPawn.summary: Lateral opposition keeps your own pawn protected when the move order is coordinated.
step.t_protectPawn: The black king is on b6 and protects c6; the white king on e7 wants to capture that pawn. The pawns are blocked. How can Black prepare a defence that still works after White’s approach?
step.t_protectPawn.hint1: Before moving closer to the pawn, check whether White can capture it immediately.
step.t_protectPawn.hint2: The pawn provides no waiting move. Look for a relationship between the kings that makes the attacker give way.
step.t_protectPawn.hint3: Compare the kings’ rank after your move and who will be able to answer the next approach.
step.d_protectPawn: Watch when c6 comes under attack and how the black king adjusts the opposition without having to abandon the defence.
step.d_protectPawn.m1: 1...Ka7. The wait leaves three squares between the kings on the seventh rank and gives White the move; c6 cannot yet be captured.
step.d_protectPawn.m2: 2.Kd7. The attacker approaches c6. The defence must now shorten the distance without giving away the favourable move order.
step.d_protectPawn.m3: 2...Kb7. The black king faces the white king on d7, with c7 between them and White to move. It also protects c6 directly.
step.d_protectPawn.m4: 3.Kd6. The white king changes ranks to renew the attack on c6. Leaving the black king on its previous square is not enough.
step.d_protectPawn.m5: 3...Kb6. The black king follows on the sixth rank and protects c6; White has to move. Keep this picture: kings on b6 and d6, with the attacker to move.
step.err_protectPawn: In this position, after 1...Kc7?, the black king moved closer to its own pawn, but now Black loses. Follow White’s reply and compare, at the end, who is to move with the earlier defence.
step.err_protectPawn.m1: 2.Ke6. The white king reaches the sixth rank; Black’s own c6-pawn prevents its king from occupying that square to obtain lateral opposition.
step.err_protectPawn.m2: 2...Kb7. The black king still protects c6, but no longer coordinates the move order as in the correct defence. Even so, there is a common trap for White: the natural 3.Kd6? attacks c6, but 3...Kb6! leaves the kings on b6 and d6 with White to move, and Black draws. 3.Kd7 or 3.Kf7 wins, leaving Black to move.
step.err_protectPawn.m3: 3.Kd7. The attacker reaches the same rank, with c7 between the kings and Black to move. Direct protection does not solve the need to make a move.
step.err_protectPawn.m4: 3...Kb6. The defender changes ranks and still guards c6; White can answer that change.
step.err_protectPawn.m5: 4.Kd6. The kings are again on b6 and d6, but Black now moves. The blocked pawns provide no waiting move; the defender must give way.
step.err_protectPawn.m6: 4...Ka7. In this continuation, the black king abandons the defence of c6. Moving away makes the effect of the unfavourable move order visible.
step.err_protectPawn.m7:
5.Kxc6. Compare the pictures with the kings on b6 and d6: in the correct defence, White was to move; in the wrong line, Black had to give way because the pawns provided no waiting move.

Before choosing the defence, check for an immediate capture. If waiting is possible, follow the attacker’s reply and the black king’s adjustment. In the resulting position, who will be to move and have to abandon the protection? That comparison determines whether bringing the king closer helps.
step.protectPawnMove.hint: Keep c6 defended by coordinating the kings’ rank and the move order. Answer each approach; do not simply choose the square nearest the pawn.
step.protectPawnMove.done: The wait 1...Ka7 prepared the defence: after each approach, your king reached the direct protection of c6 with White to move.
step.d_edgeCorner.m4: 2...Kb7. The black king shortens the distance and keeps protecting c6. Now White looks for the passage that will force it to move again.
step.d_edgeCorner.m5: 3.Kd7! The white king enters along the seventh rank, attacks c6 and leaves Black to move. Going straight to d6 would allow 3...Kb6!, with the opposition on the same rank for Black.
step.d_edgeCorner.m6: 3...Kb6. The black king protects c6 along the sixth rank. White now replies, so the approach can continue with the favourable move order.
step.d_edgeCorner.m7: 4.Kd6. The defender must move and has no pawn waiting move. Compare the two targets, c6 and c5, before choosing the next capture.
step.d_edgeCornerCapture: Going round has reached the useful point: Black has to give up the defence of one of the pawns. Watch which pawn comes within reach after this reply.
step.d_edgeCornerCapture.m1: 4...Ka5. The black king has left b6 and left c5 unprotected. In the capture, what also counts is the square from which the white king protects its own c4-pawn.
step.d_edgeCornerCapture.m2: 5.Kxc5. The white king captures on c5, keeps the pressure on c6 and stops the black king from crossing b4 and b5. The initial waiting move has turned into a concrete gain of material.
step.protectPawn:
Now the opposition must keep a black pawn, the one on c6. The white king on e7 cannot capture it yet: it first has to come closer. That gives Black time to prepare the defence instead of rushing next to the pawn.

The waiting move 1...Ka7 draws. The kings stand on the seventh rank with three squares between them and White to move. After 2.Kd7, Black replies 2...Kb7; after 3.Kd6, it replies 3...Kb6. The black king follows the attacker’s rank and keeps c6 protected.

The approach 1...Kc7? seems to reinforce c6, but loses after 2.Ke6! In the line of the mistake, the kings also reach b6 and d6; the difference is that Black has to move. Because the pawns are blocked, the king has to give up the defence of one of the pawns.

Always compare the two pictures: the protection now and the protection after the reply. The waiting move only helps when it allows no immediate capture and sets up the right turn to follow the attacker.
step.protectPawnMove: Play Black and find the best move. The white king on e7 cannot capture c6 yet.
step.diagonal.alt.e4: After this advance, Black finds a resource: the move hands Black the turn just when Black can take the direct opposition.
step.diagonal.alt.e4.m2: This resource holds the draw. With f5 between the kings and White to move, the direct opposition passes to Black.
step.capablanca.alt.kd3: After this move, Black finds a resource: the white king leaves the black king's file, and Black can take the opposition.
step.capablanca.alt.kd3.m2: This move holds the draw: the kings face each other on the d-file (going to f6 also works). With three squares between them and White to move, the opposition passes to Black, and White no longer reaches a pawn first.
step.capablanca.alt.kf3: The white king leaves the e-file on the kingside. The detour has the same flaw as the step towards the queenside: the kings are no longer on the same file, and Black, with the right move order, occupies the f-file and takes the distant opposition.
step.capablanca.alt.kf3.m2: This move holds the draw: the kings face each other on the f-file. With three squares between them and White to move, the opposition passes to Black.
step.capablancaMove.alt.kf3: With this move you let the win slip: the white king goes to the black king's file at the wrong moment, and Black answers on the same file, taking the distant opposition.
step.capablancaMove.alt.kf3.m2: This move takes the distant opposition: three squares between the kings, f4, f5 and f6, and White to move.
step.capablancaMove.alt.ke3: With this move you let the win slip: the white king returns to the e-file at the wrong moment, and Black answers on the same file, taking the distant opposition.
step.capablancaMove.alt.ke3.m2: This move takes the distant opposition: three squares between the kings, e4, e5 and e6, and White to move.
step.capablancaMove.alt.ke4: With this move you let the win slip: the white king advances too early, and Black takes the direct opposition.
step.capablancaMove.alt.ke4.m2: This move takes the direct opposition: e5 lies between the kings, and White is to move. The white king can no longer advance.
step.diagonalMove.r1: The black king moves up to d5 and tries to approach the e3-pawn.
step.defendMove.r1: The white king moves up to e4, looking to enter via d5 or f5.
step.defendMove.r2: White advances the pawn and passes the move to you.
step.lateralDefend.r1: The white king heads back to the centre along the fifth rank, to support the d2-pawn.
step.lateralDefend.r2: The white king drops to b4, still on its way to the d2-pawn.
step.capablancaMove.r1: 1...Kf8. The black king steps to the f-file, looking for another square from which to take the opposition. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Ke3? seems to keep the king in the centre, but after 2...Ke7! the kings stand on e3 and e7, with three squares between them and White to move, and Black draws with the distant opposition. Before you move, count the squares between the kings and see who will be to move.
step.capablancaMove.r2: 2...Ke7. The black king returns to the e-file, trying to face your king again. Another common trap: the natural 3.Kd4? seems to advance, but 3...Kd6! puts the kings face to face on the d-file, with one square between them and White to move, and Black draws. Look for the move that leaves an odd number of squares between the kings with Black to move.
step.outflankMove.r1: The black king goes to g6 to protect the h5-pawn.
step.edgeMove.r1: 1...Ka6. The black king moves up to a6, because it cannot stay on the fifth rank: b5 is covered by the c4-pawn. Watch out for a common trap: the natural 2.Ke5? seems to bring the king closer, but Black replies 2...Kb7! (or 2...Ka7) and draws. Think about which rank lets the white king take the distant opposition.
step.edgeMove.r2: The black king goes to b6 to protect the c6- and c5-pawns.
step.edgeCornerMove.r1: The black king retreats to a7 and waits, without losing contact with b6.
step.edgeCornerMove.r2: The black king goes to b7 and protects the c6-pawn again.
step.protectPawnMove.r1: The white king goes to d7 to attack the c6-pawn.
step.protectPawnMove.r2: The white king drops to d6 and attacks the c6-pawn again, now also close to c5.
step.diagonal.short: With 1.Kf4!, the kings stand on the diagonal with one square between them, e5, and Black is to move. After 1...Ke6, you answer 2.Ke4!, face to face, and Black must give way. 1.Ke4? Ke6 would give Black the direct opposition.
step.defend.short: In Carlsen–So (Stavanger, 2017), 55...Kf7! left three squares between the kings, f4, f5 and f6, with White to move. When the white king changed file, Black followed: 56.Ke3 Ke7 57.Kd3 Kd7. The distant opposition also serves the defender.
step.lateral.short: Euwe played 49.Kb5: the king attacks the a5-pawn and stands on the fifth rank, with three squares between the kings and Black to move. This is the distant opposition along the rank; after capturing a5, the white king returns close to the c2-pawn.
step.capablanca.short: With six squares between the kings, an even number, the side to move takes the opposition: 1.Ke2! is the only winning move. After 1...Ke7, only 2.Ke3! keeps it: three squares between the kings and Black to move. Whoever has the opposition reaches the opponent's pawn first.
step.outflank.short: Outflanking means going through the wing the enemy king has left free. 4.Kf4 keeps the opposition and protects the approach to h4; after 4...Kg6, 5.Ke5 switches the target to the b5-pawn.
step.edge.short: After 1.Kd6? Kb6!, c6 lies between the kings with White to move: a draw. The right idea is to step away: 1.Kf5! The black king cannot stay on the fifth rank, because b5 is covered by the c4-pawn; it moves up, and the white king moves up with it.
step.edgeCorner.short: 1.Ke8 Ka7 2.Ke7 leaves three squares between the kings on the seventh rank, with Black to move. After 2...Kb7, 3.Kd7! uses d7 as a passage; after 3...Kb6 4.Kd6, the black king must give way. 3.Kd6? Kb6! leaves White to move, and it is a draw.
step.protectPawn.short: The waiting move 1...Ka7 draws: the kings stand on the seventh rank with three squares between them and White to move. After 2.Kd7 Kb7 3.Kd6 Kb6, the black king keeps pace and keeps c6 protected. 1...Kc7? loses after 2.Ke6!
ex.e09.r1: 1...Kf7. The black king leaves the g-file and heads for the centre, towards e6 and d5, in front of the d2-pawn. If the white king does not follow it with the distant opposition on the new file, Black takes it, and the pawn does not get through.
ex.e11.r1: 2.Kd2. The white king changes file, heading for c3 and d3, from where it threatens to reach the key squares of the c2-pawn: b4, c4 and d4. Ask yourself on which square your king keeps the opposition after this change.
ex.e11.r2: 3.Kd3. The white king climbs to the third rank; from d3, one step takes it to c4 or d4, two key squares. There is no room left for the distant opposition: now it has to be direct.
ex.e11.r3: 4.Kc3. The white king tries from the side: from c3, it aims at b4 and c4. If your king does not stand face to face with it, a key square falls.
ex.e13.r1: 1...Kd2. The black king attacks the e3-pawn and looks for a way in through e2. Your king must defend e3 without giving up the opposition along the rank.
ex.e13.r2: 2...Kd3. The black king moves up and attacks e3 from the other side; now the entry it is looking for is e4. The idea is the same: follow it on its rank, with one square between the kings and Black to move.
rot.ideia.ex1.e1: Let's study a basic ending: king and pawn against a lone king.
rot.ideia.ex1.e2: If the pawn runs alone, the black king catches and captures it. Here your king decides.
rot.ideia.ex1.e3: Your king must clear the way for the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.e4: To do that, it heads for a key square: a square where, once your king gets there, the pawn promotes whatever the black king does.
rot.ideia.ex1.e5: For this pawn, the key squares are f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.e6: The black king wants the opposite: to stand in front of the pawn, on g6, and block your king.
rot.ideia.ex1.e7: Remember too: the kings can never stand on neighbouring squares. That is why one king blocks the other's way.
rot.ideia.ex1.p: White to move. Think and suggest a move, or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex1.certo: Exactly! Your king advances toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.revela: The best is to advance the king to e4, toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d4.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d4.2: The black king comes closer and closes the way to the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c4.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c4.2: The black king comes closer and closes the way to the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e3.1: It looks natural, but with that move White no longer wins.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e3.2: The black king goes to e7 and faces it, three squares away. Now the opposition belongs to Black.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c3.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c3.2: The black king comes closer and closes the way to the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e2.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e2.2: The black king comes closer and closes the way to the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d2.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d2.2: The black king comes closer and closes the way to the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c2.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c2.2: The black king comes closer and closes the way to the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.g3g4.1: Pushing the pawn now does not win: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.g3g4.2: The black king runs to f7 and will arrive in time in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.livre.fala: Keep playing with White and see how Black defends.
rot.ideia.ex1.livre.volta: Let's go back to the starting position. Suggest another move or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex1.fins.capturado: The black king captured the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.fins.repeticao: The black king always closes the way.
rot.ideia.ex1.fins.limite: The black king always closes the way.
rot.ideia.ex1.l1: Notice: your king went to e4, the black king's file. Now the kings are on the same file, with three empty squares between them.
rot.ideia.ex1.l2: When the kings face each other with just one square between them, that is called direct opposition.
rot.ideia.ex1.l3: The side that has just moved has the opposition: now the other king must move and give way.
rot.ideia.ex1.l4: With three squares between the kings, it is the same thing from farther away: the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex1.l5: To know who has it, count the empty squares between the kings on the same file or rank.
rot.ideia.ex1.l6: An odd number after your move: the opposition is yours. Here White has just moved the king to e4 and left three squares: the opposition is White's.
rot.ideia.ex1.l7: If it were even, the other side would step forward and leave an odd number. So, with every move, leave an odd number of squares between the kings.
rot.ideia.ex1.l8: Black has several defences. Let's start with the one that gives White the most trouble.
rot.ideia.ex1.l9: Black brings the king to f7, close to the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l10: Their plan is to reach g6 and get in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l11: You get there first: with the king on f5, you face the black king.
rot.ideia.ex1.l12: This is the direct opposition. And f5 is a key square: the black king can no longer reach g6.
rot.ideia.ex1.l13: Before going on: why not push the pawn, which looks so natural? Because the black king reaches g6, in front of it, and your king has no way to the key squares. Watch.
rot.ideia.ex1.l14: Go back one move. Imagine that, instead of taking the king to f5, White pushes the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l15: Black answers with the king on g6, right in front of the pawn. It is the ideal spot for the defense.
rot.ideia.ex1.l16: The white king tries to go around on the side.
rot.ideia.ex1.l17: The black king faces it. Now the opposition belongs to Black, and the white king cannot pass.
rot.ideia.ex1.l18: With no path for the king, White pushes the pawn with check.
rot.ideia.ex1.l19: The black king returns to the front of the pawn. It is always the same defense.
rot.ideia.ex1.l20: The white king tries the side again; the black king steps back and stays in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l21: In the end the black king has no moves, but it is not in check. That is called stalemate, and stalemate is a draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.l22: That is why the king goes first, and the pawn advances only afterwards. Let's go back to the main line.
rot.ideia.ex1.l23: Black tries again, now with the king on g7, to get in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l24: You follow with the king to g5 and face it again.
rot.ideia.ex1.l25: Another key square taken. Now the pawn advances, protected by the king, and promotes.
rot.ideia.ex1.l26: Now let's go back to the position after the first move.
rot.ideia.ex1.l27: To recap: your king is on e4, with the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex1.l28: What if Black defends another way, with the king on e7?
rot.ideia.ex1.l29: You advance to e5, facing it, and follow the black king along the side to g5. Key square taken: it is the same ending as before.
rot.ideia.ex1.l34: Let's go back to the starting position. Against the other black defenses, the idea is the same.
rot.ideia.ex1.l35: Keep the idea: the king goes in front of the pawn and wins the opposition. The pawn only advances afterwards.
rot.ideia.ex1.l36: Now let's look at the other side: how Black uses the same idea to defend.
rot.ideia.ex2.e1: Now you play Black, and the board turns around. White has just moved the king to e3.
rot.ideia.ex2.e2: With the right defence, Black holds this position.
rot.ideia.ex2.e4: The white king wants to reach f5, g5 or h5, the pawn's key squares.
rot.ideia.ex2.e5: Your king must block that path. The weapon is the same as in attack: the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.p: Black to move. Think and suggest a move, or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex2.certo: Exactly! Now the distant opposition is yours.
rot.ideia.ex2.revela: The best is to bring the king to e7: the distant opposition now belongs to Black.
rot.ideia.ex2.alt.e8f7.1: Exactly! With the king on f7, Black holds the draw.
rot.ideia.ex2.alt.e8f7.2: Let's follow the main line, with the king on e7, which wins the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8f8.1: This move loses: now White can win.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8f8.2: The white king advances and gains ground toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d8.1: This move loses: now White can win.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d8.2: The white king advances and gains ground toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d7.1: This move loses: now White can win.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d7.2: The white king advances and gains ground toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex2.livre.fala: Keep playing with Black and see how White attacks.
rot.ideia.ex2.livre.volta: Let's go back to the starting position. Suggest another move or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.coroa: The pawn promoted. Without the opposition, Black cannot hold.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.limite: The white king controls the key squares: the pawn will promote.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.repeticao: The white king controls the key squares: the pawn will promote.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.capturado: The pawn fell. Go back to the position and look for the defense through the opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.afogado: The black king was stalemated. Go back to the position and look for the defense through the opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.l1: Three squares between the kings, an odd number, and you have just moved: the opposition is yours, and White must give way.
rot.ideia.ex2.l2: White has several tries. Let's start with the most direct one.
rot.ideia.ex2.l3: White advances the king through the center.
rot.ideia.ex2.l4: You answer by facing it, on e6: direct opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.l5: White tries to go around on the side.
rot.ideia.ex2.l6: You follow to f6, always facing it.
rot.ideia.ex2.l7: With no passage for the king, White pushes the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex2.l8: Your king goes to g6, in front of the pawn: the ideal spot for the defense.
rot.ideia.ex2.l9: The white king reaches no key square. It is a draw.
rot.ideia.ex2.l10: Now let's go back to the position with your king on e7.
rot.ideia.ex2.l11: What if White tries the side right away, with the king on f4?
rot.ideia.ex2.l12: You face it again, on f6. The opposition is still yours.
rot.ideia.ex2.l13: And what if, instead of f6, you take the king to f7, near the pawn?
rot.ideia.ex2.l14: With the white king already on f4, next to f5, that loses: it steps onto f5 first, and the pawn promotes.
rot.ideia.ex2.l15: White takes advantage: the king goes to f5, takes a key square and faces the black king. The pawn will promote.
rot.ideia.ex2.l16: That is why, against the king on f4, the answer is f6: facing it, keeping the opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.l17: Let's go back to the position with your king on e7. In defense, the rule is the same as in attack.
rot.ideia.ex2.l18: Win the opposition and bring the king in front of the pawn.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.1: Now let's see the same idea with the pawn one rank further back, on the second rank.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.2: Since the pawn is one rank further back, the key squares are one rank further back too: f4, g4 and h4.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.25: The key-square rule: the square two ranks in front of the pawn and its two neighbours. It holds for pawns on the b- to g-files. The edge pawn, on the a- and h-files, follows another rule, which you will see in another lesson.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.26: With the pawn on b3, for example, the key squares would be a5, b5 and c5.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.3: Your king steps up to e3, on the same file as the black king.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.4: Count the squares between the kings: three, an odd number, and you have just moved. The distant opposition is yours.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.5: Black heads for the pawn with the king on f7.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.6: Your king reaches f4, which is already a key square.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.7: Black goes to g6 and stands in front of the pawn.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.8: You stand face to face on g4: direct opposition, on a key square.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.9: That is the winning move: you keep the opposition, and the black king has to step aside.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.10: The black king runs to the corner, and your king stays ahead of the pawn all the way to g6.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.16: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.17: What if White pushes the pawn right away, two squares?
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.18: With the pawn on g4, the key squares move up with it: now they are f6, g6 and h6, and the black king is right next to them.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.19: Black brings the king to f6 and guards the key squares.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.20: The white king comes to help, but it is too far away.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.21: The black king attacks the pawn and stands in front of it.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.22: White can only defend the pawn. The black king never leaves its path: it is a draw.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.23: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.24: With the pawn further back, the key squares drop. The king leads with the opposition; the pawn follows.
rot.demos.tempo.1: Now, thinking from Black's side: it is the same position, and the board has turned.
rot.demos.tempo.2: Only the move has changed. If Black has the move in this position, Black can organize a draw.
rot.demos.tempo.29: When having the move decides who gets the opposition, we say that side has the tempo.
rot.demos.tempo.24: How? By advancing the king to take the opposition before the white king, then standing before the pawn.
rot.demos.tempo.3: Your king steps forward to e6, toward the pawn's key squares.
rot.demos.tempo.4: Your king is close enough to answer with the opposition every time. Going to f6 also holds: the king also gets closer to the key squares.
rot.demos.tempo.5: White uses the attacking plan: the king goes to e3.
rot.demos.tempo.25: Count: two squares between the kings, an even number. Step forward and leave just one: an odd number, and the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.tempo.6: You face it on e5. One square between the kings, an odd number, and you have just moved: the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.tempo.7: From here on it is the defence of the second example: the white king tries the side, and your king always faces it, all the way to f6.
rot.demos.tempo.15: It is always the same answer: you take the opposition, and the pawn does not promote. It is a draw.
rot.demos.tempo.26: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.tempo.27: What if Black moves the king to d6, on the white king's file?
rot.demos.tempo.28: Three squares between the kings, and Black has just moved: the distant opposition is theirs. It also holds.
rot.demos.tempo.30: Notice what the black king did: it went to the white king's file. It is what your king did in the attacking example, going to e4.
rot.demos.tempo.31: When the kings are on different files, bring yours to the other king's file and leave an odd number of squares between them. As you have just moved, the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.tempo.16: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.tempo.17: What if Black moves the king to f7, close to the pawn?
rot.demos.tempo.18: Here going to f7 loses: with the pawn on g2, f4 is already a key square, and the white king gets there in two moves.
rot.demos.tempo.19: White takes advantage: the king goes to e3.
rot.demos.tempo.20: Black hurries to g6, in front of the pawn.
rot.demos.tempo.21: Too late: the white king reaches f4, a key square, and the pawn will promote.
rot.demos.tempo.22: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.tempo.23: Same position, opposite results: whoever moves first leaves the odd number, keeps the opposition and decides the ending.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.1: Now, thinking from Black's side: White moved the king to e2, not to e3.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.2: It looks like a similar step, but count the squares between the kings: now there are four.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.3: An even number: White has miscounted. Step forward and leave an odd number: the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.4: Your king advances to e6. Now there are three squares between the kings, an odd number, and you have just moved.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.5: The distant opposition is yours. Stepping to f6 also holds; any other move hands it back to White.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.7: You stand face to face on e5. It is the same position we saw a moment ago, and it is a draw.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.14: Count the squares between the kings. If your opponent left an even number, step up and take the opposition.
rot.pratica.ataque.enunciado: Play White and find the best move.
rot.pratica.ataque.fim: Your king led the way with the distant opposition, and the pawn advanced only afterwards.
rot.pratica.defesa.enunciado: Play Black and find the best move.
rot.pratica.defesa.fim: Your king took the distant opposition in time and did not let the white king through.
rot.ideia.ex1.l6b: Why? If the black king steps forward, two squares remain; your king steps forward too, and one remains. The kings face each other, and he is the one who must give way.
rot.ideia.ex1.l20b: The pawn reaches g7, but the black king is still on g8, in front of it.
rot.ideia.ex2.ponte: You have now seen the idea from both ends: in attack and in defence. Now I will play both sides and show you the same idea in other positions. In each one, notice on which square the king takes the opposition.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.10b: Only now does the pawn advance, protected by the king, and promote.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.ponte: Now it is your turn: two positions to play on your own against the machine, one in attack and one in defence. Before each move, count the squares between the kings. If they are on different files, bring your king to the other king's file.
title: Distant opposition I: the fundamentals
summary: Take the opposition from afar, reach the key squares, protect your pawn and stop the enemy king from entering.
part.wrapUp.title: To remember
part.wrapUp.summary: What to take from Part 1 and what comes in Part 2.
step.wrapUp: Remember this: distant opposition exists to reach the key square or the pawn, so choose the goal first, and in Part 2 you will see how spare tempi and waiting moves decide who has to give way.
ex.e17: Play as White and find the best move. Your king is behind the e2 pawn and the black king waits in front of it. Find the plan that wins.
ex.e17.hint: First bring the king to the centre. When Black takes the opposition you do not have to give way: there is a move that is not a king move and passes the turn.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Kd4! brings the king to the centre, on the fourth rank. After 1...Kd6, Black takes the direct opposition; that is why 2.e3! passes the turn with a pawn move. After 2...Ke6, 3.Ke4! hands the opposition back to you, and 3...Kf7 opens the way to 4.Ke5, one of the key squares of the e3 pawn. From there the win is technical.
ex.e17.r1: 1...Kd6. The black king takes the direct opposition, with one square between the kings, and it is White to move.
ex.e17.r2: 2...Ke6. The black king returns in front of the pawn, but no longer has the opposition: White spent a pawn move to pass the turn.
ex.e17.r3: 3...Kf7. With no pawn move left to pass the turn, the black king has to give way; stepping back to d7 would have the same effect.
ex.e18: Play as White and find the best move. The pawns are locked on c5 and c6 and the black king guards the rear. Find the route of your king to the enemy pawn.
ex.e18.hint: Your king should not go straight at the black king: go around it along a file it cannot reach and arrive from behind.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Kf6! starts to go around the black king. After 1...Kd7, 2.Kf7! passes through a square the black king cannot reach. After 2...Kd8, 3.Ke6! squeezes the black king, and 3...Kc7 allows 4.Ke7! It is Black to move and any king move gives way, so the white king ends up capturing the c6 pawn.
ex.e18.r1: 1...Kd7. The black king steps out to d7 and guards e6 and c7, trying to stop the white king from entering along the e-file.
ex.e18.r2: 2...Kd8. The black king steps back to d8, trying to cover e8 and e7.
ex.e18.r3: 3...Kc7. The black king returns to c7 to protect the c6 pawn.
ex.e19: Play as White and find the best move. The a-file pawns are locked and the black king is more active. Your king must reach the other side in time.
ex.e19.hint: It is a race: your king must go to meet the black king through the centre, without losing time, to get counterplay.
ex.e19.solution: 1.Kd7! starts the race against the black king. After 1...Kc5, 2.Ke6! heads for the centre; after 2...Kc4, 3.Ke5! and, after 3...Kc3, 4.Ke4! Your king arrives in time to defend and to attack the enemy pawn, and the draw is secured.
ex.e19.r1: 1...Kc5. The black king rushes to the centre and to the side of the a-file pawns.
ex.e19.r2: 2...Kc4. The black king drops another rank, threatening to enter on the queenside.
ex.e19.r3: 3...Kc3. The black king reaches c3 and threatens to go to b2 to attack the a2 pawn.
